note: Catalogues why published evaluations disagree with each other, which is the paper to read before trusting any leaderboard, including the ones we track.
title: A Systematic Survey and Critical Review on Evaluating Large Language Models
authors: Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar et al.
explain_beginner: When companies claim their AI chatbot scored well on some test, how do we know that score means anything? This paper asks why different research teams testing the same AI models so often reach different conclusions about which one is best. The authors read through a large body of published evaluation studies and cataloged the places where things go wrong. They found that many popular test sets contain mistakes in their own answer keys, that AI models sometimes get accidentally exposed to test questions before being graded on them, and that small changes in how a question is phrased can swing a model's score dramatically. They also found that using one AI model to grade another introduces its own biases, and that many published studies do not share enough detail for anyone else to redo the test and check the result. The paper does not rank any models itself. Instead it explains why leaderboards and benchmark scores should be read with real skepticism, and offers a checklist for running tests that other researchers could actually trust and repeat.
explain_business: For anyone choosing between AI models based on published benchmark scores or leaderboard rankings, this paper is a caution against taking any single number at face value. It shows that a model's position can shift substantially depending on which benchmark, which prompt wording, or which scoring script was used, so a vendor's claim of topping a leaderboard may not predict how the model performs on your actual workload. Practical implications: budget time for your own evaluation on tasks that resemble your real use case rather than relying purely on public scores, ask vendors what evaluation setup and prompt templates produced their reported numbers, and be skeptical of comparisons across different leaderboards since rankings can disagree sharply for the same pair of models. There is no new tool or product here, the value is procedural. Building an internal, repeatable evaluation process, even a simple one, reduces the risk of picking a model that looked strong on paper but underperforms in your specific application.
explain_practitioner: This is a systematic literature review, not a new evaluation method. The authors surveyed published LLM evaluation practices and organized the failure modes into three groups: reproducibility, reliability, and robustness. On reproducibility, they found only about half of the papers they reviewed released their scoring code, and details like decoding parameters and prompt templates are routinely omitted, so results cannot be independently checked. On reliability, they point to known label errors in MMLU (partly fixed by MMLU-Pro and MMLU-Redux) and missing test cases in HumanEval (addressed by HumanEvalPlus), plus contamination from pretraining data and bias in using LLMs as judges. On robustness, they show that ranking a model with one prompt template versus another, or on one benchmark versus another, can flip its relative standing, citing a case where GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro rank very differently on Chatbot Arena versus MMLU. The main limitation the authors state themselves is scope: they cover only the evaluation stage, mostly English text tasks, and exclude multimodal and multilingual evaluation.
